Dear all,

 you must be sick to death of Diode Laser questions but, forgive me, I have been out of holography for 20 years.(I still have a box of Agfa 10x 8 plates in my garage, i wonder if they will still work)

Anyway I am really impressed with the Spec and price of The D & S Laser Kit DS 650-25 for approx $250 with 35mw 658nm diode and housing. I am amazed at the 14 feet coherence length and fringe contrast, but just before I buy one, should I be considering any other 25mw+ diode laser with driver for a similar price or a little bit more? I am not too keen on very low miliwatt lasers as in the past I have found that the faster the exposure the brighter the image. i realise this is purely down to stability of the environment.

But if you give me a few days I will do a bit more testing and see what I can discover for you. It may be worth remembering than a lot of who-har is made about coherence of diodes but extremely generous coherence is only useful if you intend being either very sloppy with your path lengths or you have a very powerful laser where the object light that reflects from the back of a very deep object can return to the reference beam and still be within the acceptable ratio (a hard thing to ask unless you have a 5W argon etc.).

posts.topic_title: Is Frank's laser a good buy?
posts.author: zipsister
posts.post_subject: Is Frank's laser a good buy?
posts.content_md:
Hi Julian,

Just successfully made some diffraction gratings with the single diverging beam of the 80mW diode laser. I split off part of the beam using two mirrors that effectively increased this diverted beam by 100cm thereby giving a coherence length of at least 100cm (at least three or four times your normal coherence of a HE-NE laser). The laser diode part number is Hitachi HL-6525MG (658nm@80mW) plus the suitable power adapter was $US25. A few things to remember with reflection holograms and coherence:

With single beam reflection holograms the object has to be up close and personal with the plate; the further the object is or its parts are from the plate the less sharp it is no matter how much coherence or what laser you have. This is the advantage with split beam transfer holograms or even single beam focussed holograms; you get to focus the image at the plate, and with a narrow 'letterbox' slit included somewhere in the set-up or simply by using a narrow master hologram image to project, then you can get greater image depth and sharpness. But even here a larger coherence is only useful if recording a large object in the master stage, and as I said before you realistically use powerful lasers to light up distant parts of the object sufficiently for the correct light ratio. The bottom line is that this diode and power supply is cheap and works with good coherence. 

zipsister

I am still a little vague on the importance of coherence length. I understand that the waves need to stay in sync and that if say the coherence length is 13 cm then that is the maximum difference that the path lengths can be. Therefore I used to think that If you wanted to maximise the depth of a recorded object then you would try to make both lengths as close as possible. Some one else on another thread told me that the depth is more related to the beam ratios, in so much that in order to maximise depth then you would need to throw more light on the back of the object. Please can you explain this to me.

posts.topic_title: Is Frank's laser a good buy?
posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.post_subject: Is Frank's laser a good buy?
posts.content_md:
As you approach the edge of your coherence length you will see the object dim, then disappear. So, the coherence length or an-unstabilized HeNe is around the tube length. I always quote 6" but I have not measured this one as I am just using it for small single beams at the moment.

The problem with beam ratios is completely separate. If there is not enough light reaching the plate from the back of the scene you will not form fringes.
